The [hybrid reference](Hybrid_Tangent_Spaces.html) asks a useful question: how can local sensitivity analysis connect smooth motion, contact transitions and outcomes? Its earlier edition overstated what that analysis established. This critique also contained incorrect counterexamples, unsupported literature attributions and proposed code that repeated the reference's mistakes. A rigorous review must test the criticism as carefully as the original argument.

The corrected treatment distinguishes the physical reset, event time, common-time perturbation map, contact constraints and evidence for an application. The [accessible companion](Hybrid_Tangent_LAYMAN.html) develops the same distinctions without requiring the full derivations. This page records which objections survive, which remedies were wrong, and what would make a stronger conclusion defensible.

## 1. The Core Derivative Needs a Precise Comparison

### The Valid Objection: Event Timing Was Inconsistently Handled

For a state-triggered event, nearby trajectories generally cross at different times. The reset Jacobian alone cannot capture the difference in how long each trajectory spends in each mode. The reference now derives

$$
S=R_x+\frac{(f^+-R_xf^--R_t)h_x}{h_t+h_xf^-}.
$$

The denominator is the rate of change of the guard along the incoming trajectory, including explicit time dependence. Its nonzero value permits a local event-time derivative. The reset is evaluated at the incoming event and the outgoing field at the reset state.

The derivation must identify whether the comparison is at a common clock time or at each trajectory's own event. The earlier reference mixed those comparisons, and the critique's proposed endpoint formula added another event-time term after already using $S$. That double counted the same timing effect.

A proper check perturbs the initial state, relocates the event, and compares endpoints at the same final time after both events. Holding the nominal impact time fixed tests a different function. The new reference includes that executable comparison.

### The Rejected Objection: A Curved Guard Invalidates Saltation

A differentiable curved guard has the same first-order expansion used by the implicit function theorem. Curvature enters through the locally evaluated gradient and through higher derivatives when needed. A scalar guard need not be affine.

The relevant concerns are regularity, transversality, competing events and preservation of the local event sequence. Smooth velocity-dependent restitution is also compatible with differentiation: if $v^+=-e(v^-)v^-$, its velocity derivative is $-e-v^-e'$, not simply $-e$.

A singular reset Jacobian can still define a perfectly meaningful derivative. The matrix may be rectangular when mode coordinates have different dimensions. Invertibility is an additional requirement for particular inverse constructions, not a universal prerequisite for saltation. These distinctions accord with @Kong2023saltation.

### What Remains Difficult: Grazing and Simultaneous Events

When $h_t+h_xf^-$ approaches zero, timing sensitivity can become large. At grazing, a nearby trajectory may miss a contact or gain an additional one; a single differentiable local map may cease to describe the neighborhood.

For two nearby guards, changing the initial condition can change their order. Products $S_2S_1$ and $S_1S_2$ generally differ. A simultaneous-event model needs a physical resolution rule and an analysis of the resulting local branches. In special regular cases a derivative can exist; in others one needs directional or generalized derivatives.

The critique's proposed universal repair using a Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse was unjustified. A linear-algebra operation cannot supply an unspecified collision law, event priority or frictional feasibility condition. Likewise, replacing a guard by a tolerance band changes the model and does not by itself repair an invalid derivative.

## 2. Contact Geometry Must Agree With Mechanics

### Tangent Spaces Survive a Modeled Jump

The absence of a two-sided time derivative at impact does not erase the mode domain's tangent space. A manifold's differentiable structure and a vector field's regularity are distinct.

At a regular boundary $\phi(q)=0$, the tangent space satisfies $\phi_q\delta q=0$. For a feasible domain $\phi\ge0$, the boundary tangent cone includes directions with $\phi_q\delta q\ge0$. The incoming velocity can point outside the flow domain and trigger a reset. Flipping the cone inequality merely because one labels a state “pre-impact” confuses displacement feasibility with event direction.

### The Mass Metric Changes the Projection

For a stationary frictionless contact, impulse balance and normal restitution give

$$
P_M=M^{-1}J^{\mathsf T}(JM^{-1}J^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J,
\qquad
v^+=(I-(1+e)P_M)v^-.
$$

The projection is orthogonal in the kinetic metric: $P_M^{\mathsf T}M=MP_M$. Euclidean projection is recovered for an isotropic point mass, but not for arbitrary multibody inertia.

This distinction affects both the velocity reset and its derivatives. Differentiating a configuration-dependent reset requires the derivative of the matrix *acting on the velocity*. The original block expression omitted that contraction. An angle measured from the surface also differs from an angle measured from its normal; mixing those conventions changes sine into cosine.

With $0\le e\le1$, the energy loss is nonnegative, not necessarily strictly positive. With $e=0$ the velocity map is a projection; with $e=1$ it is a mass-metric reflection. Calling every impact a rotation or every saltation a projection conceals the timing terms.

### Friction and Support Need Their Own Conditions

The earlier particle-friction impulse omitted the restitution contribution to the normal impulse and a sticking cap. It could divide by zero or reverse tangential motion spuriously. Even the corrected particle formula has a limited domain: rotation and multibody coupling require contact-point mobility and an explicitly chosen frictional-impact law.

For sustained contact, $\dot Jv$ enters the acceleration constraint. Omitting it predicts the wrong support force for motion along a curved surface. Algebraic reaction forces must then be checked against unilateral and frictional admissibility.

A single angular-momentum equation about a foot cannot determine every joint velocity after a multibody heel strike. A planar five-link robot in free flight needs floating-base translations as well as its angles. Reduced stance coordinates are useful, but their constraints and transitions must be derived.

The critique's dismissal of small biped models was also excessive. A small model can isolate a mechanism and support numerical verification. Its value depends on a clear scope, not on whether its degree-of-freedom count resembles a particular commercial robot.

## 3. Energy Loss Does Not Prove Error Suppression

### A Counterexample in the Reference's Own Ball Model

For $e=0.8$, $v^-=-5$ m/s and $g=9.81$ m/s²,

$$
S=\begin{bmatrix}-0.8&0\\3.5316&-0.8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its eigenvalues have magnitude $0.8$. With height scaled by $1$ m and velocity by $1$ m/s, its largest singular value is about $3.7044$. It therefore amplifies some scaled perturbations in one event. The amplification concerns a difference between trajectories; it is compatible with kinetic-energy loss along each trajectory.

A full endpoint derivative also contains the flight matrices before and after contact. Neither $S^N$ with an arbitrarily fixed incoming speed nor eigenvalues from one jump represent a sequence of actual bounces.

For a declared pair of metrics, $S^{\mathsf T}W_+S\preceq\gamma^2W_-$ is a one-event differential gain bound. A trajectory or gait claim must combine those bounds with flow evolution. A periodic autonomous gait additionally has a phase direction; transverse return-map stability differs from contraction of all states at the same clock time.

### The Critique's Rotation Counterexample Was False

The earlier critique claimed that a constant factor $e<1$ multiplying rotations could fail to converge to zero because of changing rotation directions. In a compatible norm, every orthogonal rotation has norm one, so a product of $N$ such scaled rotations has norm $e^N$. It converges to zero. Commutativity is unnecessary.

More generally, a common uniform bound $\|A_j\|\le\rho<1$ gives the result directly by submultiplicativity, even for noncommuting matrices. Merely requiring $\|A_j\|<1$ separately does not supply such a uniform bound. The scalar sequence in the reference has every factor below one but a product tending to $1/2$.

The valid criticism is that actual hybrid propagation may lack a common bound and includes intervening flows. A false counterexample does not strengthen that criticism.

## 4. Zeno Behavior and Cost Require Separate Arguments

For the ideal constant-restitution ball, bounce heights and inter-event times decrease geometrically. The finite accumulation time follows from summing the flight durations. The state tends to the resting configuration, but the original flight/reset model does not specify its continuation beyond that accumulation.

The phrase “the jump set has measure zero” settles neither continuation nor sensitivity. Nor does it prove that every cost is finite. A running cost needs integrability; an event-cost sum needs convergence.

The total dissipated energy of the unforced ball is finite. A cost of one unit per impact diverges along infinitely many impacts. Both are additive event costs—the distinction is summability, not “additive versus non-additive,” as the critique previously suggested.

The critique also equated total variation with the sum of jump magnitudes. Total variation includes continuous motion. Absolute continuity within each finite flow segment and finitely many finite jumps give a useful bounded-variation trajectory under suitable boundedness conditions, but this is not a theorem for every hybrid system.

An upper bound $\Delta t_j\le C\rho^j$ gives an upper bound on the sum, not the exact accumulation time. Detecting several small numerical event intervals is likewise a practical warning, not a proof of infinitely many future events. A chosen rest completion should be physically justified and checked for convergence as numerical thresholds change.

## 5. Filippov and Complementarity Were Conflated

Filippov solutions describe a differential inclusion for an appropriate discontinuous vector field and are absolutely continuous in the usual formulation. They do not enact a velocity reset merely because an impact is instantaneous. A prescribed-time reset does not automatically require Filippov theory either.

For Coulomb friction with one common coefficient, the limiting force interval at zero velocity permits force balance. Static friction larger than kinetic friction requires a richer model. The critique's suggested interval omitted applied-force and mass factors and used a static coefficient in the moving branches without explaining the change.

Attracting versus repelling sliding depends on the signs of the two normal velocities separately. Physical tangential sliding along a contact surface is a different notion. Continuous actuator saturation has a kink, but its limiting vector-field values agree at the kink.

Complementarity notation is not restricted to linear problems. A gap-force product is a smooth function; the complementary feasible set has the difficult geometry. A general linear complementarity problem is not automatically polynomial-time solvable simply because it is linear.

Contact-implicit trajectory optimization typically becomes an MPCC with a specified contact discretization. Standard constraint qualifications can fail. Force/impulse interpretation, friction, scale, relaxation residuals and trajectory feasibility matter. Positive log terms do not make a minimization barrier, and strict positivity alone does not enforce complementarity.

The earlier proposed contact-gradient formula omitted $\dot Jv$. The proposed universal stick-to-slip saltation was also unsupported. A stick-to-slip transition can change acceleration while leaving velocity continuous; a velocity impulse must come from an actual impulse law.

## 6. Optimization Claims Need the Complete Objective and Algorithm

### Cost Timing and Second Derivatives

Changing the contact time changes the allocation of running cost between modes. Event costs can also change with state and time. The reference's accumulated-cost augmentation gives the corresponding first-order boundary term.

For a complete event-resolved map $F$ and interval cost $\ell$, an exact second derivative includes

$$
V_{xx}=\ell_{xx}+F_x^{\mathsf T}V_{xx}^+F_x
+\sum_r(V_x^+)_r(F_r)_{xx}.
$$

The last term cannot generally be replaced by zero. This is why a pullback of a quadratic value approximation and an exact second-order nonlinear DDP expansion need different qualifications.

Underactuation does not require $B$ to have full row rank for Riccati recursion. Stabilization depends on the relevant system properties and horizon. The critique's claim that floating-base systems automatically invalidate the recursion was incorrect.

### Withdraw the Invented Results, Retain the Research Question

The earlier editions stated iteration counts, runtime comparisons, a gradient table and company-specific practices without reproducible supporting evidence. Some appeared as “suggested remedies,” but their numerical presentation still looked like reported experiments. They have been withdrawn rather than converted into purported findings by changing the wording.

A defensible optimizer report identifies the model, objective, controls, constraints, parameters, initialization, timestep/event tolerances, algorithm, convergence criterion and evaluation set. Local stationarity differs from a global optimum, and optimizer convergence differs from closed-loop stability.

Adding $\epsilon I$ to $S$ changes a physical derivative. Regularizing an optimization Hessian can be useful, but its role and effect must be distinguished. A mode-discovery search is not automatically global, and a known-contact method can still vary event times or change modes under a specifically designed algorithm.

The bibliography also needed restraint. A reference about contact complementarity is not proof of the origin of saltation matrices. A paper's title or abstract cannot support an invented theorem number, complexity result or implementation claim. The revised source links identify bounded uses of the literature.

## 7. The Published Program Must Match Its Derivative

The earlier code applied `S @ x_minus` as the physical reset. Saltation maps a variation, not the nominal state. The critique's replacement code repeated this error despite explaining it correctly in prose.

A custom reverse-mode rule must describe the derivative of its own forward program. A fixed-time forward reset cannot be assigned a state-triggered derivative without changing what function is being differentiated. The critique also added a second timing derivative after $S$, and mislabeled continuous adjoint integration as a discrete adjoint.

The new NumPy example explicitly locates one bounce, applies the physical restitution rule and compares the full flow–saltation–flow derivative with independently relocated finite differences. It rejects horizons outside the one-bounce branch. Its restitution derivative is checked separately.

This verifies a manufactured mathematical example. It is not an implementation of hybrid DDP, a validation of all contact models, or evidence that a human swing has an optimal late torque reduction. Future JAX implementations should verify every claimed input derivative and their unsupported event branches in the same way.

## 8. What Would Make the Golf Argument Stronger?

The useful chain of reasoning is: actuator and passive forces shape body/club motion; that motion and contact geometry determine an incoming impact state; a contact model maps it to launch conditions; ball flight maps launch conditions to an outcome.

Each link changes the interpretation of a perturbation. Shaft flexibility can alter phase and contact orientation as well as speed. Ground support changes the body's admissible motion and reaction forces. A small change in ball position changes impact timing and potentially impact offset. A measured segment slowdown does not by itself identify energy transfer to the club.

For a proposed torque intervention, declare which input changes, what remains prescribed, what state is copied, and whether the output is measured at fixed time or at impact. Compare alternative controllers and model parameters. Report whether the intervention changes the contact sequence or produces an inadmissible event.

The two-mass collision establishes a conditional positive relationship between incoming club speed and outgoing ball speed for fixed masses, restitution and geometry. It cannot establish the best full swing under accuracy, effort, physiological or injury constraints. Likewise, a torque reduction may coexist with a club-speed increase through dynamic coupling; that coexistence does not establish causality or optimality.

The strongest next evidence would connect a declared model to repeated measured kinematics, forces, shaft/contact behavior and launch outcomes, then test predictions on data not used for calibration. Counterexamples and numerical checks sharpen the theory. Independent physical measurements determine how far that theory can explain the swing.
